hub_subtitle: From hesitant communicator to confident global business leader

lesson.menu_desc: With the investment closed and Europe on the horizon, Milton sits down with brand strategist Olivia Grant in New York to decide how American buyers should see his jewelry: not a good price, but a story. Learn the verb patterns that carry every marketing conversation — gerunds and infinitives (we avoid competing on price, we plan to open a showroom, telling our story is the key) — and the language of positioning: niche, heritage, craftsmanship, exclusivity, perception, tagline — 35 slides

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: The quality of being available only to a few people
The place a brand takes in the mind of its buyers, compared with others
The way people see and understand something
To show clearly how you are different from others
The history and traditions that a family or company passes on
A short, memorable phrase that represents a brand
A small, specific part of a market with its own type of buyer
The skill and care used to make something well by hand

items.situation: A buyer asks: What makes your jewelry different? Answer in one sentence.
Your sales manager wants a 20% discount for Black Friday. Say no politely.
Tell Olivia your plan for next year.
Describe your target buyer in one sentence.
End an email to a new boutique in a professional way.
Explain why the family history matters for the brand.

listenings.text: Hi Milton, it's Olivia. Quick update after our meeting. I spent the weekend reading about your family's workshop, and I keep thinking about that heritage. It's the strongest thing you have, so I recommend putting it at the center of everything. My team tested two taglines with ten collectors in New York. Most of them preferred the simplest one: Made by hand. Made to last. Two people said the word Brazilian made them think of beaches, not gold, so we decided to keep it in the story and out of the tagline. One more thing. I suggest stopping the online discounts this month. You can't sell exclusivity on Monday and offer twenty percent off on Friday. That damages the perception of the brand. Let's talk on Thursday. I'm looking forward to showing you the first designs.

When a new jewelry brand contacts me, I usually avoid answering the first email. That sounds rude, I know, but I get about forty emails a week from new brands. So what makes me stop and read? Three things. First, a clear niche. If you tell me you make everything for everybody, I stop reading. Second, craftsmanship I can see. I want to touch the piece, so I expect a brand to send me a sample, not a catalog. Third, a real story. Heritage sells, but only when it's true, and my customers on Madison Avenue can tell the difference. The biggest mistake I see is brands trying to compete on price. My clients don't come to me to save money. They come to own something that nobody else has. So if you want to work with a boutique like mine, stop offering discounts and start offering a reason.
